text: Given the root of a binary tree, return the values of its nodes level by level. Left to right, one list per level.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the output is a list of lists. Each inner list is one depth of the tree. So for a tree with h levels, I return exactly h lists. Is that right?

Then here is the thing I want to name up front. The output groups nodes by depth, so I have to visit nodes in depth order, not in branch order. That points straight at a queue. And there is one detail I already know will be the whole problem. A queue gives me nodes in the right order, but it does not tell me where one level ends and the next begins. I need my own way to draw that line.
Yes. Return an empty list then.
Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to two thousand nodes. Values fit in an int.

Good, two thousand is small. Let me run through the example: three, nine, twenty, null, null, fifteen, seven. The root is three, so level one is just three. Its children are nine and twenty, so that is level two. Nine has no children; twenty has fifteen and seven, so level three is fifteen, seven. That matches the expected answer.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to find the height, then for each depth walk the whole tree and collect only the nodes at that depth. That works, but it walks all n nodes once per level — order n times h, which is quadratic on a skewed tree. This problem reminds me of breadth-first search on a graph. A tree is just a graph with no cycles, so I do not even need a visited set. I will use BFS with a queue and process one full level per outer loop turn.

Here's the plan. One: push the root. Two: while the queue is not empty, freeze its size as sz — that is exactly how many nodes the current level has. Three: pop exactly sz nodes, record their values, push their children, and append that group to the answer. One thing worth flagging — I read the size once, before the inner loop starts. Inside the loop I push children into the same queue I pop from, so the size keeps changing. If the condition re-read the size every pass, the boundary would drift. It does not hang and it does not crash — it quietly blurs levels together. There's a trade-off here. A null marker after each level, or node and depth pairs, also work; the size snapshot is the cheapest, with no sentinel to handle. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. After the null guard, each outer turn freezes sz, clears the level buffer, then pops exactly sz nodes, recording each value and pushing its non-null children. One thing worth flagging — sz is an unsigned size, and my counter is an int. That compiles, but it warns under strict warnings as a signed and unsigned comparison. Could it misbehave? Only with over two billion nodes in one level, and the cap is two thousand. So it is a warning, not a bug — but casting sz to int once would make it clean.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. Same tree, expecting three; nine, twenty; fifteen, seven. Turn two is the row that matters. sz is frozen at two; I pop nine and twenty and push fifteen and seven, so at the end the queue holds the next level, and only that frozen count told me where to stop. That matches. I also ran the re-reading version over all six thousand nine hundred eighteen tree shapes up to nine nodes: wrong on six thousand four hundred six. The five hundred twelve that pass are exactly the chains, so a chain-only test hides the bug. The smallest failure is one, two, three, giving one, two; then three. Corner cases: a null root returns empty from the guard. A single node gives one list. A thousand-node chain gives a thousand one-value lists.

The time complexity is linear. Every node is pushed once and popped once, with constant work each. The space complexity is order w for the queue, where w is the widest level, not counting the output. In the worst-case scenario the tree is perfect and the bottom level holds about half the nodes. Let me think about complexity here. BFS costs width, DFS costs height, and those are opposite worst cases. On a perfect tree of a thousand twenty-three nodes, my queue peaks at five hundred twelve while a recursive DFS goes only ten frames deep. On a thousand-node chain, my queue never holds more than one node, while DFS goes a thousand frames deep. Neither is simply better. Oh, one more thing — there is zero recursion here, so a deep tree cannot blow the stack.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You named the real problem up front — a queue orders nodes but does not mark level boundaries — before you wrote a line. You quantified the size-snapshot bug instead of hand-waving it, including the point that chain tests hide it completely and the smallest failing case is three nodes. And you framed BFS versus DFS as opposite worst cases on width and height, with numbers on both shapes. Good work.
